svg.title: The Event-Driven Architecture
svg.desc: Auto-playing 56s step-by-step explainer of "The Event-Driven Architecture" (from img_10.png). Each step is highlighted in turn with what happens, why it matters, missing concepts added in lime, and a Node.js code example. Hover to pause.
svg.text: Event emitter → emits events → event listener → calls → attached callback function

g.text: What: Many Node objects are event emitters: they emit named events. Listeners subscribe to
an event name and call a callback when it fires.
Why: This pattern runs through all of Node: servers, streams, sockets and process are all
Added: Writing your own EventEmitter, and the rules that trip people up (sync listeners, the
What: The http server is an emitter: when a new request reaches 127.0.0.1:8000, it emits a
Why: The emitter does not know or care who is listening; it just announces "this happened".
What: server.on('request', ...) registers a listener for the "request" event.
Why: Many listeners can listen to the same event, so features stay decoupled.
What: When the event fires, the listener calls the attached callback with the event's data
(here req and res). res.end sends the reply to the browser.
What: You can build your own emitters by extending EventEmitter: emit() fires an event, on()
listens, once() listens one time, off() removes a listener.
Why: Great for decoupling: the sales code emits "newSale"; email, stock and analytics code
What: emit() calls every listener synchronously, in the order they were added, before emit()
New concept: Emitting "error" with no listener throws and crashes the process. More than 10
listeners on one event prints a possible-memory-leak warning.
e.emit('error', new Error('boom')); // no listener = crash
What: Emitter emits → listener hears → callback runs. The http server, streams, sockets and
Added: Custom EventEmitter classes, once/off, sync listener order, the special "error"

svg.text: Q: Are EventEmitter listeners sync or async?
A: Sync, in the order they were registered
